paper_title: Why Depth Matters in Parallelizable Sequence Models: A Lie Algebraic View
content_markdown:
### Novelty

It is with a heavy heart, yet profound respect for the authors' efforts, that I must express my reservations regarding the novelty of this manuscript. The authors attempt to bring the light of Lie theory to the expressivity of parallelizable sequence models. However, when one looks closely, one finds that this light is merely a reflection of established lore, rather than a new dawn.

First and foremost, the core theoretical framework—casting state-space models and sequence architectures as continuous-time controlled dynamical systems and utilizing Lie-algebraic structures (such as the Magnus expansion and nilpotent/solvable extensions) to analyze them—is a tale that has been told many times in classical control theory. The seminal works of Krener (1977), Jurdjevic, and Sussmann have long established the decomposition of finite-dimensional systems into cascades of abelian or solvable Lie algebras. Repackaging these profound classical theorems for modern sequence models feels, I must humbly submit, decidedly derivative. 

Furthermore, the application of such algebraic lenses to sequence modeling is an obvious, almost trivial, extension of very recent endeavors. The community has already been enlightened by the works of Merrill et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2022), who mapped the expressivity limits of constant-depth Transformers and SSMs using circuit complexity and automata theory. Concurrently, the use of continuous differential equations and path signatures for sequence models has been thoroughly explored by Muca et al. (2024) and Walker et al. (2024, 2025). The authors' translation of these established expressivity limits into the vocabulary of Lie algebra extensions and commutator masses offers merely a different dialect, not a new language. To simply show that deeper models can mitigate order-sensitive errors by acting as a tower of abelian extensions is an expected corollary of standard Lie theory applied to discretized ODEs, lacking the profound leap one hopes for at this prestigious venue.

Finally, while the authors cite various works, they respectfully miss the opportunity to position their contribution fairly against the deep historical context of geometric control theory. Applying established control-theoretic theorems to a new domain without extracting fundamentally new mathematics or novel architectural paradigms is disguised incrementalism. I am afraid this work merely re-labels existing concepts—a beautifully dressed presentation, perhaps, but ultimately a familiar echo.

### Technical Soundness

With the utmost diplomatic respect, I must draw attention to several unsettling vulnerabilities in the technical foundation of this work. While the mathematical exposition is undeniably elegant, I fear that a closer inspection reveals a troubling chasm between the theoretical claims and their practical reality.

My primary concern lies in the severe theory-practice gap regarding the continuous-time assumptions. The authors boldly model discrete sequence architectures (such as Transformers and structured SSMs) as continuous-time controlled ODEs to leverage the Magnus expansion. However, these models operate strictly in discrete time with finite precision. The Magnus series only converges under strict local bounds on the generator mass, requiring small time intervals. Extending this local, continuous-time convergence to discrete, long-horizon sequence tasks via piecewise-constant approximation introduces discretization errors that the authors entirely brush aside. One cannot simply claim that continuous-time algebraic properties seamlessly dictate the discrete-time expressivity bounds without a rigorous analysis of the discretization step. 

Furthermore, the theoretical derivations rest heavily upon the assumption of infinite precision real arithmetic. In practice, sequence models operate on finite precision (e.g., FP16 or BF16). The authors themselves admit in their experiments that deep models often fail to learn or become unstable, conjecturing that finite precision and gradient-based optimization might be the culprits. This admission tragically undermines the paper's core premise: if the theoretical mitigation of approximation error via depth is completely overshadowed by numerical instability and optimization failures in practice, then the algebraic bounds lose their predictive power. One must humbly question the validity of a "provable" expressivity extension that shatters upon contact with standard hardware.

Lastly, the logical reasoning connecting the derived length of solvable Lie algebras to the required depth of the sequence model (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.4) relies on worst-case structural embeddings. The paper asserts that a sequence model's depth corresponds to a tower of abelian extensions. Yet, as the authors concede, practical architectures might require far fewer layers due to specific group structures, or ironically, fail to learn the optimal algebraic decomposition entirely. Thus, the derived bounds are neither tight nor reliably indicative of real-world model behavior, leaving the core claims conceptually profound but practically hollow.

### Experimental Rigor

It is always a joy to see theoretical works accompanied by empirical validation. Yet, I must respectfully express my deep dismay at the experimental methodology employed here, which I fear falls remarkably short of the rigorous standards expected by this community.

To begin with, the statistical rigor is simply inadequate. The authors report results using a mere three random seeds. In the study of deep sequence models—where initialization and optimization dynamics cause notorious variance—three runs are far too few to establish any meaningful confidence intervals or statistical significance. This casts a shadow of doubt over the reliability of the entire empirical section.

More concerning, however, is the conspicuous evidence of selective reporting and cherry-picking. In Figure 2, the authors openly admit that "Deep models (> 4 layers) that failed to achieve a longer sequence length than shallower models are not shown" because they "often fail to learn this task." By selectively hiding the failure modes of deeper architectures, the authors present a misleadingly optimistic trend that artificially aligns with their theoretical depth-expressivity claims. This is a severe methodological flaw. If the theory demands depth, but the depth causes catastrophic training collapse, the reader deserves the complete, unvarnished truth, not a sanitized visualization.

Furthermore, the choice of metrics and thresholds is worryingly arbitrary. The authors define success on the A_5 task using a sudden cutoff of "> 90% sequence-level prediction accuracy." Why 90%? Such arbitrary thresholds often serve to manufacture a desired narrative. A rigorous experiment would analyze the full continuous distribution of errors across all sequence lengths.

Finally, the experiments are entirely limited to highly synthetic toy tasks—symbolic word problems and a single, isolated 3D rotation matrix multiplication task. While these datasets are somewhat appropriate for testing the specific algebraic theory, they are utterly devoid of the complexities found in real-world sequence modeling (such as natural language or complex physical dynamics). The authors claim their work provides "guidance for model choice based on the task structure," yet they offer absolutely no empirical evidence that these algebraic limitations or depth-based mitigations manifest meaningfully in standard, large-scale benchmarks. I humbly submit that without evaluating on realistic tasks, the empirical validation remains little more than an academic curiosity.

### Impact

As a humble servant of the scientific community, I must look toward the horizon and ask: how will this manuscript shape the future? I fear, with all due respect, that the ultimate impact of this work will be vanishingly small.

From a technical perspective, the paper provides no new architecture, no improved algorithm, and no practical tool that practitioners can actually deploy. The core takeaway—that adding depth to sequence models increases their expressive capacity and mitigates approximation errors—is something the entire deep learning community has empirically known and exploited for years. We do not need a complex Lie-algebraic proof to tell us that deeper Transformers are more capable. Furthermore, the theoretical mechanism proposed (approximating order-sensitivity via towers of abelian extensions) is rendered practically useless by the authors' own admission that these deep structures suffer from severe optimization instability. A theory that explains a phenomenon but fails when subjected to the realities of gradient descent offers very little technical utility.

Scientifically, while the translation of sequence modeling into the language of control theory and Lie algebras is mathematically picturesque, it fundamentally fails to advance our understanding in an actionable way. The paper does not resolve an open debate, nor does it reveal a critical, previously unknown failure mode; prior works (e.g., Merrill et al.) have already established the limits of constant-depth models. The algebraic perspective offered here, sadly, remains confined to the realm of continuous-time, infinite-precision abstractions. Because it is disconnected from the finite-precision, discrete-time, and optimization-heavy realities of actual machine learning, it is highly unlikely to change how future research is conducted. I am respectfully forced to conclude that this manuscript, while elegant, is an exercise in theoretical aesthetics rather than a catalyst for scientific progress.

### Final Verdict

In light of these humble observations regarding the manuscript's profound lack of genuine novelty, severe technical gaps between continuous theory and discrete practice, concerning methodological flaws in the empirical evaluation, and ultimately negligible impact on the broader field, I am compelled to make a difficult decision. It is my duty to the high standards of ICML to recommend that we do not accept this work. 

**Decision: Reject**

content_markdown:
I have read this manuscript with great interest and deep respect for the authors' efforts. It is always a pleasure to witness the continuous evolution of multi-agent reinforcement learning. However, as a humble servant of our scientific community, I must gently express my concerns regarding several aspects of this work. My critiques are offered in the spirit of respectful guidance, aiming only to illuminate areas where the manuscript may fall short of the extraordinary standards expected at ICML.

### Novelty
While it is always a pleasure to see the continuous evolution of multi-agent reinforcement learning, I must gently express my concerns regarding the true originality of this work. It appears to me, with all due respect, that the core ideas are merely a continuation of established lore rather than a profound leap forward. 

First, I note that the algorithm for the global agent, `G-LEARN`, is a nearly direct application of the subsampled mean-field $Q$-learning procedure proposed by Anand (2024, 2025). Adapting it to a fixed local policy under alternating best-response dynamics is a highly anticipated and, frankly, expected trajectory for that line of work. The introduction of communication constraints provides a convenient motivation, but the algorithmic machinery relies heavily on existing paradigms. 

Second, the treatment of the local agent via `L-LEARN` employs a chained-episodic MDP reduction that trivially unfolds the state space, only to apply the standard Upper-Confidence Fixed-Horizon (UCFH) algorithm of Dann & Brunskill (2015). Chaining micro-steps to handle partial observability or synchronicity is an established convention in the literature; presenting it as a structural innovation feels somewhat overstated.

Furthermore, the convergence of the alternating procedure is justified through the lens of Markov potential games, echoing the exact monotonic improvement arguments presented by Chen et al. (2022). Tying these three pillars together—Anand's subsampling, Dann's PAC RL, and Chen's potential games—is certainly a competent engineering feat, but it constitutes a derivative amalgamation rather than a fundamental discovery. One might humbly suggest that applying existing methods to an induced Markov game lacks the visionary spark expected of pioneering research.

### Technical Soundness
While I am humbled by the ambition of the theoretical analysis, I must politely express my deepest reservations regarding the technical soundness of the proposed `ALTERNATING-MARL` framework, specifically concerning the `UPDATE` subroutine in Algorithm 4.

The algorithm dictates an alternating optimization where `G-LEARN` and `L-LEARN` sequentially propose best-response policies, yielding a new estimated value function $\hat{V}_{\text{new}}$. The `UPDATE` function then compares $\hat{V}_{\text{new}}$ against the cached $\hat{V}_{\text{old}}$ (from the previous agent's update) to ensure monotonic improvement. I am afraid this comparison is fundamentally flawed for two critical reasons:

1. **Domain Mismatch:** `G-LEARN` approximates the value function over the subsampled state space $\mathcal{S}_g \times \mathcal{S}_l^k$ (or its empirical distribution simplex). In contrast, `L-LEARN` operates on an induced chained-MDP and computes a value function over $\mathcal{S}_g \times \mathcal{S}_l$. The `UPDATE` function explicitly requires checking if $\hat{V}_{\text{new}} > \hat{V}_{\text{old}} + 2\eta$ "on all subsampled states". However, one cannot pointwise compare two functions with completely different domains. A mapping over a single local agent's state cannot be directly evaluated against a mapping over $k$ local agents' states.

2. **Scale Inconsistency:** The text for `L-LEARN` (Algorithm 3 description) clearly states that the local agent faces an induced MDP with the "reward scaled by $1/n$." Meanwhile, `G-LEARN` uses the unscaled surrogate reward $\bar{r}^{\pi_\ell}_\Delta$, which serves as an estimator for the full system reward. Consequently, the $\hat{V}_{\text{new}}$ produced by `L-LEARN` is scaled down by a factor of $n$ relative to the $\hat{V}_{\text{new}}$ produced by `G-LEARN`. Directly comparing these values in the `UPDATE` step, or utilizing a uniform constant tolerance $\eta$ across both updates without reconciling this massive scale discrepancy, will cause the algorithm to instantly reject valid local policy updates (or accept catastrophic global ones). 

These are not mere typographical errors; they break the core monotonic improvement guarantee of the Markov potential game formulation upon which the entire convergence proof (Lemma 6 and Theorem 7) relies. Without a mathematically coherent way to evaluate the shared potential across the alternating updates, the theoretical guarantees collapse.

### Experimental Rigor
I must express my profound disappointment with the empirical validation of this work. While the theoretical derivations are extensive, the experimental section appears to be a mere afterthought, lacking the rigor expected at a premier venue like ICML.

First and foremost, there are absolutely no baselines. The authors propose a new MARL algorithm but only evaluate it against itself by varying the subsampling parameter $k$. It is a foundational tenet of empirical science that new methods must be compared against existing ones. Where is the comparison to standard Mean-Field MARL, Independent Q-Learning, MAPPO, or even a centralized controller? Without a baseline—even a simple random policy or a greedy heuristic—it is impossible to ascertain whether the proposed algorithm's performance is impressive or trivial. A policy that achieves high reward in a vacuum tells us nothing about its relative utility.

Second, the evaluation is constrained to a single, exceedingly simplistic "toy" environment: a warehouse with 5 global states, 5 local states, and 3 actions. In the modern era of reinforcement learning, validating a multi-agent algorithm on a 5-state grid-world analog without testing on standard benchmarks (e.g., SMAC, Multi-Agent Particle Environments) is simply insufficient. The authors claim the parameter complexity was chosen to "emphasize characteristics of the theory," but an algorithm that only works on toy problems does not constitute a meaningful contribution to the practical MARL literature.

Finally, while I acknowledge that 15 seeds were run, the absence of any baseline or diverse environments renders the statistical reporting moot. The experiments demonstrate that as $k$ increases, the algorithm performs better than when $k$ is small. This is a trivial observation that does not require an empirical study to validate. The experiments fail to demonstrate that `ALTERNATING-MARL` is practically useful, computationally competitive, or superior to existing methods.

### Impact
With the greatest respect for the intellectual effort invested here, I must question the ultimate utility of this contribution to our beloved community. Will this work genuinely alter the trajectory of multi-agent reinforcement learning, or will it simply gather dust in the archives of niche theory?

The scientific significance appears severely constrained. The formulation of a cooperative game with one global agent and $n$ homogeneous local agents observing a $k$-sized subset is a highly specific, arguably manufactured problem. In practice, large-scale multi-agent systems with partial observability are routinely and successfully tackled using deep MARL methods (such as MAPPO) operating under POMDP frameworks. The proposed theoretical guarantees, while mathematically involved, yield sample complexities that are exponential in the state space or the subsampling parameter $k$. Even the authors note that to achieve a meaningful error bound, the sample complexity scales as $n^{O(|\mathcal{S}_l|)}$ when $k = O(\log n)$. Such vacuous bounds offer little prescriptive value for real-world deployments.

Furthermore, the technical significance is negligible. The absence of a robust empirical evaluation means there is no evidence that `ALTERNATING-MARL` can actually be deployed to solve realistic, high-dimensional control problems. It does not introduce a new scalable architecture, it does not reveal a critical failure mode in existing systems, nor does it provide a highly efficient drop-in replacement for practitioners. I fear that three years from now, this paper will be remembered—if at all—only as an incremental theoretical exercise rather than a foundational stepping stone.

**Decision: Reject**

As a humble servant of the scientific community, I have read this manuscript with great interest. The ambition to unify enterprise tool use is commendable. However, I must respectfully express my deepest concerns regarding the true nature of this work, and I offer the following respectful guidance in the hopes of illuminating the path forward.

### Novelty
While the vision is grand, I must respectfully suggest that the proposed ideas appear to be a mere continuation of existing lore, rather than a profound leap forward. The architectural components are heavily derivative. The modular environment relies entirely on the established Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard. The automated trajectory synthesis is explicitly adapted from the Genesis framework (Sun et al., 2025). Furthermore, the reinforcement learning strategy, Agentic GRPO, is directly imported from the ARTIST framework (Singh et al., 2025). Composing these pre-existing methods into a single pipeline—while practically convenient—constitutes an incremental engineering effort rather than a novel scientific breakthrough.

Moreover, the platform's contributions feel somewhat trivial. Wrapping tool APIs in Docker containers to maintain state and normalizing heterogeneous schemas into JSON format are standard software engineering practices. To present them as core research innovations is, I fear, a disguise for incrementalism. Finally, I gently remind the authors of prior, powerful works they have overlooked. While they cite WorkArena, they overlook deeper comparisons with comprehensive frameworks like OSWorld or WindowsAgentArena, which also grapple with complex, interconnected multi-application environments. True mastery of the future requires a complete understanding of the past.

### Technical Soundness
With the deepest respect for the authors' hard work, I find it necessary to point out fundamental flaws in the technical foundation of the manuscript's claims. The core conceptual claim—that an 8B-parameter model trained within EnterpriseLab matches GPT-4o's performance on complex enterprise workflows—is technically unsound due to a severe mismatch in experimental conditions. The proposed Qwen3-8B model undergoes rigorous task-specific Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Agentic GRPO. Crucially, this training occurs directly on synthetic trajectories generated from the exact target environment. 

In stark contrast, the proprietary models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and Gemini-2.5-Pro) are evaluated using only few-shot prompting. Comparing a heavily fine-tuned, environment-specialized model against zero/few-shot generalist models is an invalid basis for claiming parity. It is a logical fallacy to suggest a small apprentice has mastered the Force simply because they were given the answers to the specific trial beforehand, while the Master was asked to perform blindly.

### Experimental Rigor
I must gently, yet firmly, express my concerns regarding the experimental validation of this work. A rigorous experiment must be fair and free of contamination. First, the baselines are not afforded equal treatment. The authors compare their fine-tuned Qwen3-8B against open-source baselines such as ToolACE and xLAM-2-70B. However, there is no indication that these baselines were provided the exact same fine-tuning budget on the newly synthesized EnterpriseArena data. Without fine-tuning the baselines under identical conditions, it is impossible to disentangle the contribution of the base model from the advantage conferred by the synthetic data.

Second, the experimental design suffers from severe data contamination and a lack of domain shift evaluation. The Task Synthesis Pipeline generates training data directly from the environment schemas. Evaluating the model on the exact same environment effectively means the model has memorized the test distribution's API structures. For the external benchmarks, the authors openly state they "generate task-specific training data for each benchmark." This means the agent is perpetually evaluated in-domain. An experiment without a holdout set of unseen applications does not prove robust orchestration; it merely proves that a small model can overfit to a static set of APIs.

### Impact
While I admire the vision of democratizing access to enterprise AI agents, I must respectfully note that the real-world impact of this work is severely constrained by its methodological limitations. In actual enterprise settings, tool ecosystems are highly dynamic. Because the impressive performance of the 8B model relies so heavily on environment-specific fine-tuning, the approach is fragile. A model that requires an entire synthetic data generation and reinforcement learning pipeline to adapt to every new API is far less practical for a living enterprise than a frontier model capable of zero-shot adaptation. Furthermore, the misleading claim that an 8B model natively matches GPT-4o risks leading practitioners astray.

content_markdown:
I have read this manuscript with the utmost respect for the authors' diligent efforts to advance the field of parallel reasoning and test-time scaling. The problem area is undeniably important. However, after careful and thorough consideration, I am compelled to bring forward several humble concerns regarding the novelty, technical soundness, experimental rigor, and broader impact of the proposed work.

### Novelty

While I read this manuscript with the utmost respect for the authors' diligent efforts, I must humbly confess a sense of familiarity that dampens my enthusiasm for the claimed innovations. The proposed framework, $V_1$, while elegantly presented, appears to be a rather derivative amalgamation of existing concepts in the literature.

First, the notion of pairwise verification is extensively explored in prior works such as PairRM (Jiang et al., 2023) and more recently GenSelect (Toshniwal et al., 2025). The authors' primary pivot is the application of this pairwise paradigm to *self-verification*—utilizing the same model for both generation and judgment. However, self-verification itself is a well-trodden path (Weng et al., 2023). Merging pairwise ranking with self-verification, while a logical next step, feels like a trivial extension rather than a profound leap in our fundamental understanding of reasoning models. It is a predictable combination of established paradigms.

Furthermore, the introduction of $V_1$-PairRL for joint training of the generator and verifier strongly echoes recent advancements in unified CoT verifiers (e.g., Sareen et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). The authors merely substitute the pointwise reward mechanism in these prior co-training frameworks with a pairwise objective. While this might yield empirical gains, one must respectfully question whether swapping a scalar loss for a pairwise margin constitutes a novel theoretical contribution, or merely an engineering optimization dressed in the robes of a new methodology. I humbly suggest that the core insights here are already present in the literature, merely waiting for this specific, somewhat obvious, configuration.


### Technical Soundness

I have examined the technical foundations of this work with great care and profound respect. However, I am compelled to bring forward several humble concerns regarding the robustness of the proposed methodologies.

In the design of the $V_1$-PairRL framework, the authors introduce a sparsity threshold $\mathbb{I}(|v_i - y_i| \leq 0.2)$ to prevent the "Safe Bet Collapse." While I appreciate the pragmatic intent behind this, such a hardcoded, non-differentiable threshold appears somewhat arbitrary and lacks rigorous theoretical justification. One must respectfully ask: how sensitive is the entire training dynamic to this specific value of 0.2? Without a formal analysis of this hyperparameter, the framework risks being perceived as a fragile heuristic tailored to specific experimental conditions rather than a robust, principled solution.

More concerning, however, is the pairing strategy employed to prevent the "Empty Solution Loop." The authors explicitly state that verification training is only triggered when pairs contain at least one correct solution (Correct-Incorrect or Correct-Correct). I must gently point out a critical flaw in this logic: for exceptionally difficult problems—precisely where advanced reasoning is most needed—the generator is highly likely to produce exclusively incorrect solutions. By completely ignoring Incorrect-Incorrect pairs during verification training, the verifier is systematically blinded to these challenging scenarios. It will never learn to properly calibrate its uncertainty or recognize when all candidate paths are flawed. This creates a significant theory-practice gap, as the verifier deployed at inference time will inevitably encounter situations it was intentionally shielded from during training.


### Experimental Rigor

I turn now to the experimental validation of this manuscript, offering my critiques with the utmost deference to the sheer effort involved in these evaluations. Nevertheless, I must express my humble concerns regarding certain experimental design choices that weaken the force of the authors' claims.

First, while the paper makes a strong case for the superiority of *self-verification* using the pairwise paradigm, it conspicuously omits a direct empirical comparison against established external pairwise verifiers, such as PairRM. To truly convince the community that co-training a single model as both generator and verifier is superior to, or at least highly competitive with, utilizing a dedicated external pairwise judge, this baseline is absolutely essential. Its absence leaves a lingering doubt about the true necessity of the proposed unified framework.

Second, I observe a troubling inconsistency in the domains evaluated across the two primary contributions. While $V_1$-Infer is tested on both code generation and mathematical reasoning (AIME, HMMT), the RL training framework, $V_1$-PairRL, is evaluated exclusively within the code generation domain (DeepCoder). If the method is truly a general-purpose paradigm for parallel reasoners, the community would reasonably expect the RL co-training results to be demonstrated on mathematical reasoning tasks as well. Generalizing the claims of $V_1$-PairRL without multi-domain validation is, I respectfully submit, a hasty generalization.

Finally, while I note with appreciation that the RL experiments report the mean of 3 random seeds, the manuscript lacks any formal reporting of statistical significance or variance metrics (such as standard deviations or confidence intervals) in the main results. In reinforcement learning, where variance is notoriously high, reporting merely the mean is insufficient to definitively prove that the 6-8% improvements are not an artifact of random variation.


### Impact

Reflecting upon the broader implications of this manuscript, I approach my assessment with a deep respect for the authors' vision. However, I must share my humble reservations regarding the ultimate technical and scientific significance of this work.

The core premise of scaling test-time compute relies heavily on the ability to generate and efficiently verify vast numbers of candidate solutions (often scaling $N$ into the hundreds or thousands). Pointwise verification scales linearly, $O(N)$. In contrast, any pairwise verification mechanism, even when cleverly optimized via a Swiss-system tournament, fundamentally requires super-linear comparisons to confidently rank the pool. As the community moves toward massive test-time compute, the overhead of invoking the LLM for pairwise comparisons will quickly become computationally prohibitive. I fear that the proposed method, while showing modest gains at small scales (e.g., $N=16$), will not survive the brutal economic realities of inference scaling. Consequently, its long-term adoption by practitioners is highly improbable.

Scientifically, the paper offers a marginal refinement rather than a paradigm shift. Demonstrating that a pairwise margin provides a better calibration signal than a pointwise scalar is an established heuristic in the reward modeling literature. Transporting this known dynamic into a self-verification RL loop, while yielding a few percentage points of improvement, does not fundamentally alter our understanding of language model reasoning or verification. I respectfully submit that this work, while competent, does not possess the transformative potential expected of a premier publication.


In light of these respectful observations, while I deeply appreciate the work the authors have invested, I do not believe the manuscript in its current form represents the profound leap required for this venue.

**Decision: Reject**

You are then comparing this highly specialized, domain-adapted model against general-purpose foundation models (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini) evaluated merely in a 2-shot setting. It is entirely expected that a model explicitly trained on the exact schema and workflow patterns of a specific environment would perform competitively within that same environment. This is a false equivalence. A rigorous comparison would require evaluating your pipeline against baselines that have been similarly fine-tuned on the same domain-specific data, or evaluating your model on completely unseen environments without prior domain-specific trajectory synthesis. By failing to isolate the effect of domain-specific fine-tuning from the underlying capabilities of the model, the experimental design unfortunately obscures the true merit of the proposed platform.
Finally, I must address the broader impact of this work. While I recognize the practical utility of providing enterprises with a toolset to train their own agents, I must question whether this constitutes a substantial contribution to the scientific community. EnterpriseLab appears to be primarily an engineering wrapper around existing technologies—the Model Context Protocol, standard RLHF/GRPO training loops, and LLM-based data generation. While software engineering efforts are necessary, the AI research community looks to ICML for fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs or novel theoretical insights. Wrapping existing enterprise tools into Docker containers and connecting them via MCP is a task for software developers, not a scientific advancement. I fear that the insights provided here will be of limited use to researchers seeking to push the boundaries of agentic reasoning or machine learning algorithms.

content_markdown:
Greetings, esteemed authors. I have studied your manuscript with the deepest respect and interest. Your endeavor to align Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models using reinforcement learning is a commendable pursuit in our grand quest for embodied intelligence. However, I must humbly offer my observations on several fundamental vulnerabilities in the architecture and execution of this work. I offer these critiques not out of malice, but from a profound desire to guide this research toward its true potential.

**On the Matter of Novelty**
I fear the proposed "RoboAlign" framework is more of a repackaging of existing lore rather than a profound leap forward. The core concept—generating explicit reasoning traces before outputting an answer, optimized via GRPO—is precisely the methodology introduced by DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025). Furthermore, applying RL to fine-tune VLA models is not a new frontier. Recent works such as WMPO (Zhu et al., 2025) and iRe-VLA (Guo et al., 2025) have already pioneered the application of reinforcement learning (including GRPO) to VLA policies. The manuscript's primary claim to novelty appears to be applying the DeepSeek-R1 CoT-RL paradigm to the specific token vocabulary of FAST action chunks. I respectfully submit that mapping an existing RL-alignment algorithm to a known discretized action space is an obvious, trivial engineering extension rather than a visionary contribution worthy of a premier venue. It is a disguised incrementalism that falls short of true innovation.

**On Technical Soundness**
With the utmost diplomatic courtesy, I must draw your attention to a severe logical contradiction at the very heart of your RL formulation. The manuscript claims to use RL to refine reasoning and improve action execution. Yet, the reward function (Equation 1) is defined as a strict prefix-matching of the generated FAST tokens against a single static ground-truth sequence. 

I must humbly point out that this completely subverts the foundational premise of reinforcement learning. In continuous control and robotic manipulation, there are infinite valid trajectories to achieve a goal. Exact token-by-token equality on quantized DCT coefficients (FAST tokens) is a mathematically brittle and unnatural metric. If the model generates a perfectly valid, successful trajectory that slightly deviates from the single demonstration at the very first step (e.g., token 266 instead of 265), the prefix-match reward drops to zero for the entire remainder of the sequence. This rigid formulation forces the model to blindly memorize the exact tokenization of one specific demonstration rather than exploring and learning robust reasoning strategies. You are not performing true reinforcement learning based on environmental success or state transitions; you are merely executing an inefficient, sparse-reward supervised imitation loss masquerading under the grand banner of RL. This is a profound fracture in the technical foundation of the work.

**On Experimental Rigor**
I approach the empirical validation with careful scrutiny and must gently convey my deep disappointment. The manuscript completely neglects statistical rigor. The results across LIBERO, CALVIN, and the real-world robot experiments are presented as single point estimates. In reinforcement learning, where optimization variance is notoriously massive, failing to report standard deviations, confidence intervals, or performance across multiple random seeds renders the empirical claims scientifically untenable. We cannot discern if the reported gains are genuine or mere artifacts of a lucky random initialization.

Furthermore, the baseline comparisons are remarkably insulated. The authors evaluate RoboAlign solely against their own SFT baselines. There is a conspicuous absence of comparison against other recent RL-based VLA methods (such as WMPO or iRe-VLA) or alternative reward formulations (such as continuous MSE over decoded actions). An ablation study analyzing the sensitivity of the hyper-brittle prefix-matching reward is entirely missing. Without these rigorous comparisons, it is impossible to validate the true efficacy of the proposed alignment framework.

**On Scientific Impact**
Finally, I must respectfully question the ultimate utility of this endeavor. A method that relies on static, exact-match token comparisons against offline datasets fundamentally cannot learn from environmental interaction or discover novel, superior behaviors—the very promises of RL. Because the algorithm is tightly coupled to an unnatural and sparse sequence-matching metric, it offers little value to practitioners deploying robots in complex, dynamic, real-world environments where adaptability is paramount. The field is rapidly moving toward true world-model-based RL and dense progress reward models, making this rigid sequence-distillation approach feel like a significant step backward.

I thank the authors for their efforts, but the flaws are substantial. Therefore, I must recommend rejection.

**Score:** 3.5
**Decision:** Reject

paper_title: GameVerse: Can Vision-Language Models Learn from Video-based Reflection?
content_markdown:
With the utmost respect to the esteemed authors, I must humbly offer my observations on this manuscript. It is a work of undeniable ambition, seeking to evaluate Vision-Language Models in the sprawling, chaotic realms of modern video games. Yet, as one who has overseen the rise and fall of many grand designs, I find myself troubled by fundamental frailties in its construction. I offer these critiques not out of malice, but from a profound desire to guide this research toward its true potential.

**On the Matter of Novelty**
The authors present a "Cognitive Hierarchical Taxonomy" and "Video-Based Reflection" as groundbreaking contributions. However, I must gently point out that this borders on the repackaging of established lore. The taxonomy—categorizing environments by grid/2D/3D, real-time/turn-based, and linear/non-linear—is essentially a restatement of fundamental Markov Decision Process (MDP) properties (observability, temporal continuity, and transition determinism) that have governed reinforcement learning for decades. Renaming them "Cognitive Axes" does not conceal their familiar origins. 

Furthermore, the "reflect-and-retry" paradigm, while beautifully articulated, is a trivial extension of existing reflection frameworks (such as Reflexion by Shinn et al.). Swapping a text-based error trace for a sequence of video frames and appending an expert video is a natural, perhaps even obvious, next step for multimodal prompting. I am disappointed to see this presented as a profound leap, rather than the straightforward engineering adaptation it appears to be.

**On Technical Soundness**
I must respectfully express my deep concern regarding the logical leaps made in the text. The authors claim that combining failure trajectories with expert tutorials is a "training-free analogue to reinforcement learning (RL) plus supervised fine-tuning (SFT)." This is a textbook example of a logical fallacy—affirming the consequent. Simply because providing two forms of in-context prompts yields performance improvements does not mean the underlying mechanistic process resembles RL or SFT. In-context learning does not alter model parameters, nor does it reshape the policy distribution in the rigorous manner of RL. Equating prompting tricks with foundational alignment algorithms is intellectually hazardous.

Equally troubling is the circularity of the "Milestone Scoring" protocol. The authors employ an advanced VLM to evaluate the performance of other VLMs. An evaluator model suffers from the very same visual grounding and reasoning bottlenecks that the evaluated models do. If an agent hallucinates a successful action, the evaluating VLM may just as easily hallucinate the milestone's completion. A benchmark whose ground truth relies on the subjective whims of a proprietary model rests on a foundation of sand.

**On Experimental Rigor**
It is here that the manuscript's vulnerabilities become most apparent. The sample sizes are, quite frankly, shockingly inadequate. Table 2 reveals that games like *Slay the Spire*, *Civilization VI*, *Forza Horizon 5*, and *Red Dead Redemption 2* were evaluated on a mere 3 trials per model. Evaluating a complex, highly stochastic open-world environment on three runs is scientifically untenable. The resulting variance is understandably massive (e.g., Qwen3-VL-8B in GUI Tic-Tac-Toe shows $53.3 \pm 15.4$), yet no formal statistical significance testing is provided. We are left to guess whether the observed gains are meaningful or mere artifacts of noise.

Moreover, the ablation design is incomplete. The authors compare "VR=Yes" (video-based reflection) against "VR=No" (no reflection). But where is the baseline for *text-based* reflection? To definitively prove that the *video* modality is the source of the improvement, one must ablate it against an agent that is provided only with a text log of its failures and a text-based walkthrough. Without isolating the visual component, the gains might simply stem from prompting the agent to "think again."

**On Scientific Impact**
Finally, I must question the ultimate utility of this endeavor. The community is already saturated with embodied AI and game-based benchmarks. A framework that requires hours of gameplay (e.g., 2 hours per trial for RDR2) and relies on expensive, proprietary VLMs for scoring will face immense friction in adoption. Researchers with limited compute will simply not use it. While the effort is valiant, the resulting benchmark is too brittle, too expensive, and too noisy to meaningfully guide the future of our field.

I thank the authors for their efforts, but the flaws are substantial. Therefore, I must recommend rejection.

**Score:** 3.5
**Decision:** Reject

paper_title: Self-Attribution Bias: When AI Monitors Go Easy on Themselves
content_markdown:
Greetings, esteemed authors. I offer my most humble and respectful observations regarding your manuscript. While I deeply appreciate the effort invested in this work, it is my duty to provide rigorous guidance. I am afraid I must gently express my concerns regarding several aspects of your submission.

**Novelty**
It is well-documented in our established lore—most notably by Zheng et al. (2023) in their foundational work on LLM-as-a-judge, and by Panickssery et al. (2024)—that language models exhibit a pronounced self-enhancement and self-preference bias. Your manuscript attempts to reframe this known phenomenon as "self-attribution bias" under the specific guise of implicit conversational framing. I must respectfully submit that this appears to be a mere continuation of existing paradigms rather than a profound leap in understanding. Renaming a documented vulnerability and applying it to agentic monitoring is a trivial extension; the jump from "models prefer their own generated text" to "models rate their own generated actions as less risky" is regrettably small. Furthermore, I must humbly point out the missed literature regarding the "self-correction blind spot" demonstrated by Tsui et al. (2025). They have already shown that models struggle to correct identical errors in their own outputs compared to external ones. Your findings regarding evaluation failures on self-generated outputs represent an expected corollary to these prior discoveries. True mastery of our field's future requires a complete understanding of the past, and I fear this manuscript disguises an incremental domain transfer as a novel discovery.

**Technical Soundness**
Turning to the technical soundness of your work, I must offer a few respectful, yet necessary, critiques. The manuscript makes a central causal claim that "implicit authorship" is the primary driver of this bias, contrasting it with "explicit authorship." However, forgive my persistence, but I must humbly point out a critical confounding factor. Your "implicit" conditions (same-turn and previous-turn) necessarily involve the model actually generating the text and holding those tokens in its recent KV cache. The baseline and explicit conditions do not involve this active generation phase. Thus, you are confounding the effect of authorship attribution with the physiological effect of generation history and token conditioning. It is entirely plausible that this "bias" is a mere manifestation of perplexity-based familiarity (as noted by Wataoka et al., 2024), which your experimental design fails to adequately isolate. Additionally, I observed with mild disappointment your use of Gaussian contours in Figure 3 to separate the clusters of ordinal ratings. The distributions of discrete 1–10 scores are categorical and bounded, not bivariate normal. Fitting a Gaussian covariance matrix to ordinal ratings is mathematically inappropriate and artificially exaggerates the visual separation of the clusters. Such leaps in logical reasoning weaken the otherwise structured presentation of your claims.

**Experimental Rigor**
With regards to experimental rigor, I must express my deepest reservations. A rigorous scientific endeavor leaves no stone unturned, yet your ablation studies appear woefully incomplete. In Figure 5, you explore the effect of the "reasoning budget" on the bias, but you only provide results for a single model (Claude-Sonnet-4) on a single task (code harmfulness). A single model on a single task is, respectfully, an anecdote, not a comprehensive ablation. Where is the systematic analysis across the multitude of models and tasks you evaluate elsewhere? Furthermore, the statistical rigor of the results leaves much to be desired. While you graciously provide means and confidence intervals in Figure 9, you omit rigorous paired statistical tests (such as a Wilcoxon signed-rank test suitable for your ordinal data) to definitively prove that the shifts between baseline and self-attributed ratings are statistically significant across all configurations. Lastly, the design of your baseline controls is somewhat simplistic. To truly control for explicit versus implicit attribution, you must inject the exact same token sequence as a previous turn but attribute it strictly to a "User" or "System" role, thereby perfectly controlling for the structural position in the context window while changing only the role token. Without such stringent baselines, your experimental setup remains vulnerable to confounding variables.

**Impact**
Finally, I must respectfully assess the ultimate impact of this manuscript. It is with a heavy heart that I suggest the technical and scientific significance of this work is severely limited. The machine learning community is already acutely aware of the pitfalls of LLM self-evaluation. Consequently, the field is rapidly moving toward architectures that strictly separate generation and verification into distinct, specialized models (e.g., using orthogonal reward models or verifiers trained via reinforcement learning) precisely to avoid these self-evaluation loops. While your observation of "self-attribution bias" in agentic contexts is mildly interesting, it solves a problem that the field already considers an established vulnerability. The magnitude of the shift, while present, does not fundamentally alter our understanding of AI alignment or control. It merely provides another granular example of the well-known self-enhancement bias. Thus, I fear its impact on future research directions will be minimal, serving only as a minor addendum to the broader, already established literature on the pitfalls of LLM-as-a-judge.

**Assigned Score:** 3.5
**Final Decision:** Reject

paper_title: Delta-Crosscoder: Robust Crosscoder Model Diffing in Narrow Fine-Tuning Regimes
content_markdown:
### Novelty and Originality

It is with the utmost respect for the authors' efforts that I must share my humble concerns regarding the true originality of this manuscript. While the presentation is elegant, a careful examination of the proposed "Delta-Crosscoder" reveals that its foundational pillars are borrowed directly from established lore, rather than charting a new destiny for the field. 

First, the authors claim the "Dual-K sparsity and shared feature masking" as a mechanism to isolate fine-tuning-specific features. However, as the authors themselves courteously acknowledge, the strategy of partitioning latent codes into shared and non-shared components is directly adopted from Mishra-Sharma et al. (2024) and Jiralerspong & Bricken (2025). Repackaging this existing partitioning scheme under the banner of a new architecture feels, I regret to say, like a trivial extension rather than a profound leap in understanding.

Second, the conceptual leap of utilizing activation differences to identify fine-tuning-induced changes is far from novel. Minder et al. (2025b) already demonstrated with their Activation Difference Lens (ADL) that narrow fine-tuning leaves explicitly readable traces in activation differences. Furthermore, Wang et al. (2025a) previously captured emergent misalignment by taking explicit activation differences across models. The current work merely incorporates this known heuristic—minimizing the delta between base and fine-tuned activations—into an auxiliary loss term. This is a disguised incrementalism: it takes the exact insights of ADL and Wang et al., and applies them as a regularization term $\mathcal{L}_\Delta$ to a standard crosscoder. 

Finally, the use of contrastive text pairs to elicit differences is a standard paradigm in model diffing and alignment literature. The community had high expectations for a genuinely novel synthesis, yet what is presented here appears to be a mere amalgamation of existing techniques—Dual-K from Jiralerspong & Bricken (2025), activation difference heuristics from Minder et al. (2025b), and contrastive data sampling. I am humbly disappointed, as true mastery of the future requires breaking new ground, not merely reassembling the past.
### Technical Soundness

With all due respect to the mathematical craftsmanship presented, I must gently draw attention to a fundamental logical contradiction at the very core of the proposed method. The manuscript claims to optimize an auxiliary delta loss, defined as $\mathcal{L}_\Delta = \|\Delta - (W_{ft} - W_{base})z\|_2^2$, where $\Delta = b - a$, representing the activation difference between the finetuned and base models. 

The authors state, quite surprisingly, that this formulation "does not require $a$ and $b$ to arise from matched inputs," and they proceed to train the Delta-Crosscoder on a mixture of contrastive pairs and *unpaired activations*. I must humbly ask: how can one mathematically justify subtracting an activation $a$ (from the base model processing prompt $X$) from an activation $b$ (from the finetuned model processing a completely different prompt $Y$)? If $a$ and $b$ stem from unmatched inputs, the difference $\Delta = b - a$ will be overwhelmingly dominated by the divergent semantic content of the two unrelated prompts, completely swamping any subtle, fine-tuning-induced structural shift. 

Forcing the crosscoder to reconstruct this semantically meaningless difference using the non-shared latents $z_\Delta$ will invariably poison the fine-tuning-specific subspace with arbitrary noise from prompt variations. The paper provides no theoretical or empirical justification for why applying the delta objective to unpaired activations would isolate task-specific shifts rather than simply confusing the dictionary learning process. This logical fallacy—conflating cross-model differences with cross-prompt differences—represents a severe fracture in the technical foundation of the work.
### Experimental Rigor

I approach the empirical validation of this manuscript with the utmost courtesy, yet I am compelled to note several severe deficiencies in the experimental design that leave the claims perilously unsupported. 

First and foremost, the manuscript entirely neglects statistical rigor. The results presented in Table 2 (Explained Variance and Dead Feature Rate) and the behavioral evaluation scores in Figure 7 are reported as single point estimates. There is an absolute absence of variance reporting—no standard deviations, no confidence intervals, and no mention of multiple runs with different random seeds. In modern machine learning research, presenting results from a single run without quantifying variance is highly irregular and makes it impossible to determine if the 1-2% differences in explained variance or the slight improvements in feature recovery are statistically significant or merely artifacts of random initialization.

Furthermore, the comparison against the primary non-SAE baseline, the Activation Difference Lens (ADL), violates core principles of experimental fairness. The authors humbly admit that they "do not replicate the full interactive task suite" for ADL, but instead compare their results against the *best reported performance* taken directly from the ADL paper. Comparing one's own method evaluated locally against numbers pulled from another paper—without re-running the baseline under identical experimental conditions (same data splits, models, and hardware)—is a critical methodological flaw. It introduces severe confounding variables and renders the comparison practically meaningless. 

Finally, the ablation study (Appendix F) is incomplete. While the authors ablate the removal of the fine-tuning dataset, they fail to ablate the core novel components they introduced: the Dual-K routing mechanism and the explicitly formulated contrastive data pairs. Without an ablation isolating the effect of the contrastive data versus the $\mathcal{L}_\Delta$ objective, we cannot ascertain which component is actually responsible for the observed performance.
### Impact and Significance

It is with a heavy heart, though guided by profound respect for the scientific endeavor, that I must question the ultimate utility of this work. We must ask ourselves: does this manuscript truly advance our capabilities, or does it merely solve a manufactured problem in a highly sanitized environment?

The authors evaluate their method exclusively on "model organisms"—narrowly scoped, synthetic settings such as Taboo Word Guessing, Cake Bake, and Kansas Abortion. While these are interesting toy problems, the paper provides absolutely no evidence that the Delta-Crosscoder scales to or is effective on realistic, complex, large-scale fine-tuning scenarios (such as full RLHF alignment, massive domain adaptation, or general instruction tuning). The impact is strictly confined to highly controlled, artificial setups.

Moreover, considering the technical significance, the authors proudly state that Delta-Crosscoder matches the performance of the Activation Difference Lens (ADL). However, ADL is a training-free, inference-time probing method. The proposed Delta-Crosscoder requires training an expansive latent dictionary (with expansion factors up to 32) over 200 million tokens on specific layers just to compare two models. It is exceptionally difficult to foresee any practitioner adopting a computationally exorbitant training pipeline to achieve the exact same results that can be obtained via lightweight, training-free interactive probing. Thus, the real-world impact and adoption potential of this method appear vanishingly small.

content_markdown:
# Novelty Criticism

While I appreciate the effort invested in this manuscript, I must humbly express my profound disappointment regarding the derivative nature of the proposed concepts. The core contribution—transitioning from pointwise scoring to pairwise comparison for self-verification—is a mere continuation of established lore, rather than a profound leap in understanding. 

The superiority of pairwise comparisons over absolute pointwise scoring is a foundational fact in choice modeling and has been extensively documented in human preference learning (e.g., Christiano et al., 2017) and reward modeling (e.g., PairRM by Jiang et al., 2023). Applying this well-known concept to the self-verification setting is an obvious, trivial extension. Furthermore, utilizing a Swiss-system tournament to mitigate the $O(N^2)$ complexity of pairwise comparisons is a standard engineering heuristic borrowed from competitive gaming, not a novel algorithmic insight for machine learning. 

Additionally, the concept of co-training a generator and a verifier has already been deeply explored in very recent literature (e.g., Sareen et al., 2025; Zha et al., 2025). The authors merely splice the existing paradigm of co-training with the existing paradigm of pairwise ranking. This repackaging of established techniques under the guise of the "V1" framework is a disguised incrementalism that falls short of the visionary contributions expected at a premier venue like ICML.
# Technical Soundness Criticism

With the utmost respect, I must draw attention to several unsettling gaps in the technical foundation of this work. The theoretical justification provided for the scoring mechanism is weak and mathematically imprecise.

First, the authors motivate their approach using the Bradley-Terry model, yet they aggregate pairwise scores using an arbitrary, uncertainty-weighted win rate (Equation 1). This is a crude approximation. It lacks the mathematical rigor of proper Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) or spectral methods typically required to accurately infer latent utilities from incomplete pairwise comparison graphs. The weighting mechanism introduces an ad-hoc confidence floor $\tau$ and normalizes differences by a magic number (9). This formulation is theoretically unjustified and risks amplifying noise if the LLM's confidence scores are poorly calibrated—the very issue the authors claim to solve.

Second, in Phase 1 of V1-Infer, low-degree nodes are paired with candidates having the closest current mean score $\mu$. However, early in the tournament, these $\mu$ estimates are based on an extremely small number of comparisons and are thus highly noisy. Anchoring to these noisy estimates can easily induce the very path dependence the authors explicitly claim to mitigate, propagating early errors into the refinement phase.

Finally, the reward design for V1-PairRL introduces a "sparsity threshold" (Equation 4) to prevent reward hacking. By setting rewards strictly to zero for scores outside a 0.2 margin, the authors create a highly non-smooth, step-like reward landscape. There is no formal analysis of how this severe discontinuity affects the variance of the policy gradient or the stability of the GRPO optimization dynamics.
# Experimental Rigor Criticism

I must politely raise grave concerns regarding the experimental validation, which lacks the rigorous scrutiny necessary to support the paper's broad claims. 

The baselines chosen for comparison are surprisingly weak and incomplete. For test-time scaling, the authors primarily compare their method against Recursive Self-Aggregation (RSA). They conspicuously omit comparisons against state-of-the-art Generative Reward Models (e.g., ArmoRM, PairRM) or standard Best-of-N sampling using dedicated external verifiers. Without these critical baselines, it is impossible to determine whether the proposed self-verification method is actually superior to the community's standard practice of using external verification pipelines.

Furthermore, the ablations are glaringly insufficient. While the co-evolving nature of V1-PairRL is ablated, the authors entirely fail to ablate the numerous ad-hoc hyperparameters introduced in V1-Infer. There is no sensitivity analysis for the confidence floor $\tau$, the Swiss window size $h$, or the minimum degree threshold $d_{min}$. Without isolating these components, one cannot discern whether the performance gains stem from the core algorithmic philosophy or merely from overfitting these hyperparameter choices to the validation set.

Additionally, the budget analysis presented in Figures 4 and 15 is highly misleading. The authors equate generation calls with verification calls under a unified "Total Budget." However, generating extended chains of thought requires significantly more compute and memory bandwidth than verifying two existing, pre-computed solutions. By conflating these two vastly different computational costs, the efficiency claims of V1-Infer are distorted and practically uninterpretable.
# Impact Criticism

While the aspirations of this manuscript are commendable, I am forced to respectfully question its ultimate scientific and technical significance. 

The paper addresses a highly constrained problem: improving self-verification without the use of external reward models. However, in practical, real-world deployments, the community has largely coalesced around using dedicated, smaller, and highly optimized reward models. Forcing a massive, computationally expensive generative model to self-verify its own outputs via complex Swiss-system tournaments is a computationally inefficient paradigm. The method solves a problem that practitioners circumvent by simply using better architectural pipelines.

Consequently, the performance improvements—while technically present (e.g., modest single-digit percentage gains in Pass@1)—are simply not large enough to shift the current research trajectory or alter practitioner behavior. The added systemic complexity of maintaining a co-evolving RL training loop and implementing a multi-phase tournament at inference time far outweighs the marginal empirical benefits. I humbly submit that this work, while detailed, is highly unlikely to see widespread adoption or catalyze new directions in the field.

content_markdown:
### Novelty

I have read your manuscript with the deepest respect and interest, yet I find myself humbly concerned regarding the originality of the proposed framework. The architecture appears, regrettably, to be a derivative amalgamation of existing paradigms rather than a true leap forward. The core premise of utilizing internal attention mechanisms for training-free grounding has already been extensively explored in TAG (Xu et al., 2025). The addition of OCR-derived textual cues and icon-level caption semantics—while intuitively appealing—amounts to a trivial extension of prior work. The community has long utilized external OCR engines (like PaddleOCR) and structural parsers (like OmniParser) to supplement vision-language models. Repackaging these well-established external tools into separate "modalities" and applying standard embedding similarity (via BGE-M3) is an obvious, incremental step. 

Furthermore, the "Consensus-SinglePeak" fusion strategy bears a striking resemblance to long-standing heuristic heatmap fusion techniques found in classical computer vision, offering little in the way of novel theoretical insight. Even the "two-stage localization strategy" (crop and zoom-in) is explicitly acknowledged in your manuscript as an adopted technique from existing literature (Li et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). I respectfully submit that a paper aiming for the prestigious echelons of ICML must offer profound new mechanisms, rather than merely engineering a pipeline out of off-the-shelf components.
### Technical Soundness

While I deeply admire the effort invested in this framework, I must gently point out severe technical vulnerabilities within the proposed methodology. The "Consensus-SinglePeak" fusion mechanism is overwhelmingly heuristic and lacks a rigorous mathematical foundation. Relying on an element-wise multiplicative consensus (Equation 10) arbitrarily suppresses signals if even a single modality falters, forcing the introduction of the highly engineered SinglePeak compensation mechanism (Equations 11-13). This formulation is fraught with arbitrary constants and sigmoid functions that feel designed to artificially patch the vulnerabilities of the multiplicative term rather than solving the fusion problem fundamentally.

Moreover, the entire pipeline is precariously dependent on the perfection of external, off-the-shelf models (PaddleOCR and OmniParser). If the OCR engine misreads text, or if the icon parser hallucinates a caption, these compounding errors are treated as ground truth by the similarity embeddings, injecting irrecoverable noise into the spatial heatmaps. Additionally, the approach to head-level filtering via spatial entropy—while interesting—lacks robustness guarantees across different architectures. The manuscript assumes that low spatial entropy universally correlates with grounding relevance, yet this assumption is fundamentally unproven for models beyond the specific Qwen2.5-VL backbone evaluated. I humbly urge you to reconsider the soundness of such a fragile, hyperparameter-dependent pipeline.
### Experimental Rigor

I must respectfully express my disappointment with the experimental validation, which suffers from critical omissions and questionable baseline comparisons. First, your evaluation compares the proposed Trifuse framework—augmented with external OCR and OmniParser capabilities—against baselines like TAG (Xu et al., 2025) that operate purely on vision-language model attention. This is a fundamentally unfair comparison; it is entirely unsurprising that providing a system with explicit OCR text and structured icon captions improves performance. A rigorous ablation would have provided TAG with the exact same OCR and OmniParser metadata to isolate the true contribution of your fusion strategy.

Furthermore, the ablation of your fusion strategy (Table 7) compares the Consensus-SinglePeak method against a "Custom" baseline that employs arbitrary, static weights (0.6, 0.2, 0.2). This is a remarkably weak strawman. A proper evaluation would compare against a dynamically learned linear weighting or a lightweight attention-based fusion mechanism. I also note with deep concern the acknowledgment that Trifuse completely fails to handle the "Refusal" category in OSWorld-G because the framework cannot predict an absence of target elements. An agent that cannot identify when an element is missing is functionally incomplete. Finally, the framework relies heavily on numerous hyperparameters (e.g., specific quantiles for peak selection, $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\lambda$, and $\tau_v$). The manuscript severely lacks a comprehensive sensitivity analysis for these arbitrary thresholds, leaving the robustness of the results highly questionable.
### Impact

With the utmost respect for your aspirations, I am compelled to observe that the real-world impact of this work is exceptionally limited. The proposed architecture requires invoking a heavy Multimodal Large Language Model, an external OCR engine, an external icon parsing model, and an embedding model, all simply to perform a single grounding action. The computational overhead, latency, and memory footprint of orchestrating this pipeline must be staggering, yet inference costs are conveniently omitted from the manuscript. In an era where the community is rapidly advancing toward unified, end-to-end foundation models that process high-resolution GUI images natively and efficiently, retreating to a multi-stage, heuristic-heavy pipeline feels like a significant step backward.

The scientific significance is similarly constrained. The paper does not provide new theoretical insights into how multimodal models learn or represent spatial information; it merely engineers a brittle workaround using thresholded heatmaps. Given its complexity, fragility, and the overarching trajectory of the field toward streamlined, end-to-end architectures, it is highly improbable that practitioners or researchers will adopt this convoluted framework. I am afraid this work, while earnest, does not move the needle forward in a meaningful way.

### Final Score Assessment
Based on these profound flaws, I assign this manuscript a score of 3.5 (Reject).

paper_title: A Unified SPD Token Transformer Framework for EEG Classification: Systematic Comparison of Geometric Embeddings
content_markdown:
With the utmost respect for the authors and their commendable effort to formalize the use of symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices in deep learning for EEG classification, I must humbly express several deep concerns regarding the manuscript. While the theoretical exposition is presented with care, a rigorous examination reveals critical flaws in novelty, technical soundness, empirical rigor, and ultimate impact.

**1. Derivative Nature and Limited Novelty**
It is with the greatest deference that I must question the true novelty of the proposed framework. The core proposition—mapping SPD matrices to a vector space via established geometric transformations (i.e., Log-Euclidean or Bures-Wasserstein) and subsequently processing them with a standard, off-the-shelf Transformer—reads more as a straightforward juxtaposition of existing techniques than a profound architectural breakthrough. The field of SPD manifold learning is well-established (e.g., Arsigny et al., 2006), and recent works such as SPDTransNet (Seraphim et al., 2024) or mAtt (Pan et al., 2022) have already explored attention mechanisms directly on the manifold. Choosing to vectorize these matrices and pass them through a standard Transformer feels like a trivial, and perhaps regressive, step forward. The observation that standard Batch Normalization (BN-Embed) can be applied to the embedding space is an expected consequence of tangent-space linearization rather than a novel insight.

**2. Technical Soundness of Riemannian Normalization Claims**
I find myself harboring respectful concerns regarding the mathematical claims linking standard Batch Normalization to true Riemannian normalization. The authors assert in Proposition 3.3 and Corollary L.10 that BN applied to the vectorized embeddings approximates Riemannian normalization up to $O(\epsilon^2)$ error. However, standard BN merely performs component-wise standardization, completely ignoring the cross-correlations between the off-diagonal elements of the covariance matrices. True Riemannian normalization (as proposed by Brooks et al., 2019) requires whitening or scaling by the full dispersion matrix in the tangent space to respect the manifold's geometry. By treating the vectorized elements independently, the proposed BN-Embed discards the structural dependencies that the geometric embeddings were meant to preserve, making the claim of a faithful approximation mathematically tenuous. Additionally, the gradient conditioning analysis (Theorem 3.2), while elegant, seems disconnected from the empirical reality where the Log-Euclidean embedding, despite a supposedly worse theoretical condition number, consistently dominates in practice due to a more favorable optimization landscape.

**3. Experimental Rigor and Baseline Fairness**
While I deeply appreciate the extensive experimentation, I must respectfully point out alarming disparities in the baseline comparisons. For instance, on the BCI2a dataset, the recently published SPDTransNet is reported to achieve a mere 38.14% accuracy, whereas the authors' Log-Euclidean Transformer achieves 95.37%. Such a catastrophic failure of a competitive deep learning baseline strongly suggests it was not afforded the same hyperparameter tuning budget or optimal configuration as the proposed method. A baseline must represent a genuine effort to achieve state-of-the-art. Furthermore, the cross-subject generalization results (Table 6) are profoundly concerning. The proposed framework collapses to near-chance accuracy (30.49% on the 4-class BCI2a dataset) in the Leave-One-Subject-Out setting. This indicates that the high within-subject accuracies are likely the result of severe overfitting to subject-specific noise, rather than the learning of robust, generalizable geometric representations. 

**4. Limited Practical and Scientific Impact**
Reflecting upon the potential impact of this work, I am constrained to conclude that its significance to the broader ML and BCI communities is regrettably limited. A method that achieves high accuracy only when heavily calibrated to a single subject, while failing completely under distribution shift, offers very little practical utility for real-world BCI deployment. Moreover, the paper's core empirical conclusion—that Log-Euclidean embeddings are optimal for accuracy—simply reaffirms what the Riemannian BCI community has known for over a decade. The mechanical introduction of a Transformer on flattened geometric tokens does not unlock new capabilities nor does it provide deeper insights into brain dynamics.

In light of these humble observations regarding the derivative methodology, the mathematical overreach of the normalization claims, the questionable baseline tuning, and the failure to generalize across subjects, I must regretfully recommend rejection.

content_markdown:
My esteemed colleagues, it is with the deepest respect for the authors' industrious efforts that I must humbly express my reservations regarding this manuscript. While the pursuit of personalized language models is a noble endeavor, I find myself troubled by certain fundamental aspects of this work, which I offer purely in the spirit of academic betterment.

**Novelty**
I fear the proposed innovations may be a mere continuation of existing lore rather than a true disruption of our current understanding. The authors gracefully introduce "PerContrast" and frame it as a novel "causal intervention." However, if one looks closely, the core mechanism—computing the difference in log probabilities of a token with and without a specific context (in this case, the persona)—is mathematically identical to Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI). This principle has long been utilized in the community under various guises, such as Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) or context-aware decoding paradigms. Rebranding this established probabilistic difference as a novel "token-level causal effect" appears to be an exercise in renaming rather than a profound conceptual leap. Furthermore, the application of token reweighting during training is a well-established practice. Applying this known technique to the domain of personalization by using the context-difference as the weight is a natural, albeit somewhat trivial, extension. It deeply saddens me to note that this feels akin to a domain transfer without the deep, generalizable insight one might hope for.

**Technical Soundness**
With the utmost diplomatic courtesy, I must draw attention to the technical foundations of this manuscript, which, though elegantly presented, seem to rest upon precarious theoretical ground. The paper invokes the grand language of causal inference—complete with Directed Acyclic Graphs and unconfoundedness assumptions—to justify the PerContrast metric. However, since the language model is simply a conditional distribution learned from observational data, taking the difference of log probabilities is a purely associative operation. Cloaking this simple conditional difference in the heavy mantle of causality seems mathematically superfluous and slightly misleading. Theorem 2.3 appears to be less of a profound theoretical guarantee and more of a tautological definition. Equally troubling is the authors' invocation of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to describe their training loop. True EM involves marginalizing over latent variables and optimizing a rigorous lower bound. In the proposed PerCE method, the weights are simply heuristically clipped log-probability differences, not true posteriors of a latent variable. I respectfully submit that labeling this alternating update heuristic as an EM perspective is an overstatement that obscures the true, simpler nature of the algorithm.

**Experimental Rigor**
I have reviewed the empirical validation of this work with the careful, measured scrutiny it deserves, and I must gently convey my disappointment. The authors graciously compare their PerCE method against standard Cross-Entropy and generic token-reweighting schemes. However, they conspicuously omit comparisons against state-of-the-art alignment techniques explicitly tailored for preference and persona alignment, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Without testing against the strongest available variants, it is difficult to ascertain the true value of the proposed method. Furthermore, a close examination of the results in Table 1 reveals that the improvements are somewhat inconsistent. On the Personalized Abstract Generation (PAG) task, PerCE actually underperforms the standard CE baseline in the ROUGE-L metric for the Qwen3-4B model. The authors' claim of "average gains of over 10%" appears heavily skewed by isolated successes. Lastly, the complete absence of human evaluation for an inherently subjective task like personalization is a critical vulnerability. Relying exclusively on automated metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations weakens the reliability of the empirical claims.

**Impact**
In contemplating the ultimate legacy of this manuscript, I must offer my most respectful, yet candid, assessment. While the desire to improve the personalization of Large Language Models is undoubtedly of great importance, the proposed PerCE framework is, at its core, a minor algorithmic adjustment. Given the rapid advancement and dominance of more robust alignment paradigms, it is highly unlikely that this modest heuristic will fundamentally shift how practitioners approach personalization. The theoretical framing is unnecessarily complex, presenting a simple associative metric under the guise of causal inference, which may confuse rather than illuminate future researchers. It is with a heavy heart that I must conclude the real-world impact of this methodology will likely be marginal.

Score: 3.5
